div.head: WAR
div.p: THE WAR

Tax paralysis which seemed to fall upon the Russian arum on the occasion of the remark- able Turkish victory at Floras appears, day by day, to proclaim itself with more com- pleteness. The case hae been strikingly stated by the correspondent of the Dolly News writing recently from Biala, to whose estimate of the situation we may usefully refer. Re warns us that the reinforeement of the Russian army must take more time than has been supposed, and that, in conse- quence of this tact, the war cannot be con- eluded this year. Great battles will be fought, but only north of the Balkans. The hope of being able to advance on Adrian- ople must be postponed, and the aim of the Russian generals will now be to sweep Bul- garia north of the Balkans clear of the Turkish armies. The passel; of the Balkans, we are told, will be held, a very strong posi- tion being taken up at Keeanlik. The noceeeity of thus restricting operations south of the Balkans arises from the aspect of affairs north of that range. The eorrespon- dent represents the Russians there as unable to move. They must wait for reinforcements. A. hundred thousand men are coming; but they must be waited for. In accordance with this view, the blow with which Onelan Paella is threatened cannot be struck, be- cause troops are not available in numbers sufficient to deliver it. The right flank of the Russian army is suffieiently protected, but the means are utterly inadequate for a renewed offoneive. The correspondent gives very specific reasons for believing that the Ruesians are not in a position to strike at the forces of Eyoub Parka and Mehemet All Pectin; at the beet they can only stand on the defensive. The correepondent in question declares that what has happened at elevna has altered the whole plan of the campaign. I No more reckless, if victorious, raids now. INo more advances, regardless of threaten- ing concentrations on the flanks. The 'Russians have virtually abandoned the ex- pectation of pressing the war successfully across the Balkan.. For this year it will suffice them if during the three months still available for fighting they can sweep Bul- garia north of the Balkans clear of the Turkish armies. The Crescent must wave over the towers of Adrianople and the waters of the Golden Rum for yet another winter." Commenting on these statements the Daily Nous is of opinion that they show that it is in the power of a Government dispos- ing of as many troops as that of Turkey to give to the war a character in respect of method and duration altogether different from that which the Russian Government desired to impress upon it. Very soon, in- deed, after the commencement of the war we were warned,by events not to expect a , rapid succession ot crises, but the Turkish I commanders have now made a short war imposeible. It was never very likely that we should see a repetition of the Seven Weeks' War of 1866, but now we may ex- pect to witness something not unlike the great Civil War in America— n war slow in its processes, ex- hanging in its methods, and terminating in the utter collapse of one of the belligerents. After discussing the serious monetary strain that prolonged military operatio swill cause to Russia, and the practical bankruptcy under which the Ottoman Govelnment is notoriously labouring, the wrier c .ncludes with an observation which will command general eintellirenee. Neither the Russian nor the Turkish Government is disposed to rest content with anything short of a com- plete success; and remembering how long this Eastern Question has weighed upon Europe, and the necessity that exists for its decisive solution, we believe that the larger interests of the world will be served by this uncompromising attitude of the belligerents.
